hypothesis: 15(R)-17-phenyl trinor PGF2α isopropyl ester is increased or characteristic in 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants
rationale: Searches confirm that this feature is not an endogenous human metabolite: CAS 130273-87-9 is a synthetic phenyl-substituted prostaglandin analog, described by chemical vendors and reference sources as the 15(R)-epimer of the latanoprost/bimatoprost isopropyl ester and specifically as a known process impurity of the latanoprost bulk drug product (an ophthalmic FP-receptor agonist). No primary study - human, animal, infant, or adult - was found reporting this compound in stool, gut, or any developmental/dietary metabolomics context, let alone comparing 5- vs 12-month-old infants. The only relevant literature retrieved is at the class/pathway level: endogenous prostaglandins (PGE2, PGF2α and its 13,14-dihydro-15-keto metabolite) are consistently detectable in human milk across lactation stages, which gives a purely theoretical rationale for higher F-series prostaglandin-like signal in more milk-dominant 5-month-old infants than in 12-month-olds who have transitioned to a more solid, complementary-feeding diet. That reasoning concerns native PGF2α, not this 17-phenyl-trinor isopropyl ester, and no study links milk prostaglandin intake to infant fecal prostaglandin levels by age. Because something class-relevant but nothing feature- and group-specific was found, this scores 1 (weak) rather than 0. The most likely interpretation of such a spectral match in an untargeted lipidomics run is a library-driven misannotation (METLIN/lipid database hit at m/z of C26H38O5) of an isobaric endogenous oxylipin/prostanoid or other lipid species, so the directional hypothesis cannot be evaluated against literature on the named compound.

evidence.title: 15(R)-17-phenyl trinor Prostaglandin F2α isopropyl ester (CAS 130273-87-9) - Cayman Chemical
evidence.study_population: Not a study population; chemical reference/product record
evidence.relevance: Establishes compound identity: a synthetic latanoprost-related isomer (15-epi bimatoprost isopropyl ester) described as a potential impurity of latanoprost, i.e., a xenobiotic drug-related molecule rather than an endogenous infant gut metabolite.

evidence.title: CAS 130273-87-9 15(R)-17-phenyl trinor Prostaglandin F2α isopropyl ester - BOC Sciences
evidence.study_population: Chemical catalog record citing in vitro/ocular pharmacology literature (porcine/rabbit ocular tissue)
evidence.relevance: Corroborates that documented literature on this exact compound concerns ocular prostaglandin-analog pharmacology and latanoprost manufacturing impurities, with no gut, fecal, dietary, or pediatric context.

evidence.title: Prostaglandins in human milk
evidence.study_population: Six healthy term nursing mothers (colostrum, transitional, mature milk); human
evidence.relevance: Indirect, class-level support only: shows PGE2 and PGF2α are present in all fresh human milk samples, providing a theoretical basis for greater F-series prostanoid exposure in milk-dominant younger infants; does not address this synthetic analog or infant fecal levels by age.

evidence.title: Prostaglandin E1, E2, and F2 alpha in human milk and plasma
evidence.study_population: Lactating women (human milk and maternal plasma)
evidence.relevance: Further class-level corroboration that PGF2α is present in human milk at concentrations exceeding plasma; still indirect, as it neither measures infant gut/stool prostanoids nor the named 17-phenyl trinor isopropyl ester.

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Healthy infants across the complementary feeding period, first year of life
evidence.relevance: Confirms that infant gut microbiome and associated metabolites shift substantially between early milk-based feeding and later complementary feeding, the biological contrast underlying the hypothesis - but this study reports no prostaglandin-analog features, so it cannot support the specific direction for this feature.

caveats: The named compound is a synthetic pharmaceutical analog/impurity, so a genuine biological presence in infant stool is implausible unless the infant or mother was exposed to latanoprost/bimatoprost; treat the feature as a probable Level-2/3 (putative) annotation of an isobaric endogenous prostanoid or oxylipin (C26H38O5, MW ~430.6) rather than a confirmed identification. MS/MS confirmation against an authentic standard, or re-annotation against endogenous prostaglandin libraries, is needed before interpreting any 5- vs 12-month difference. Evidence cited for the prostaglandin class comes from human milk composition studies, not from infant fecal metabolomics, so the directional link (milk-derived prostanoids -> higher fecal signal at 5 months) is untested. Vendor/catalog pages were used only for chemical identity, not as biological evidence.
